webTitle: Kamala Harris is belatedly courting progressives. Is it too little, too late? | Arwa Mahdawi

fields.headline: Kamala Harris is belatedly courting progressives. Is it too little, too late?
fields.trailText: As she mulls another presidential run, the former VP is building bridges with progressive and Arab American leaders
fields.bodyText: Does Donald Trump secretly want Republicans to get annihilated in the midterms? Because he’s certainly acting that way. He continues to brush off concerns about the cost of living, saying last week that high gas prices are a very “inexpensive price to pay” for the war on Iran. And, of course, the president seems to have no plans to end that disastrous war, apart from making vague threats about blowing the entire country up. Trust me, he keeps saying, everything will get better after the midterms. But by the looks of his dismal polling numbers, not many people are swallowing his empty promises anymore. Still, despite the mess the Republicans have made of the country, I wouldn’t feel too optimistic about the Democrats returning to power: the party is famous for snatching defeat from the jaws of victory. Instead of evolving, it has a tendency to do the same thing over and over again, expecting different results. See, for example, the fact that there are once again loud murmurings that Kamala Harris plans to run for president in 2028. The former vice-president hasn’t made any sort of official announcement yet – she told voters in Detroit this week that she’s still deciding what to do – but she seems to be testing the political waters through midterm campaigning. This week she flew to Michigan, one of the states she lost to Trump in 2024, to join the Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed at a roundtable focused on Black maternal health. Harris will also be campaigning with the senator Jon Ossoff in Georgia next month and attending an event in Las Vegas with the Nevada attorney general, Aaron Ford, for his gubernatorial bid. Harris’s appearance in Michigan wasn’t some spur-of-the-moment attempt to be helpful; it was a highly calculated move designed to put her back on the national political stage. The New York Times reported this week that Harris’s aides had circulated a donor prospectus in July “that showed how she would try to maintain her influence atop the Democratic Party as she considered another run for president in 2028”. The document, which solicited funds for campaign travel, explained how Harris could boost midterm candidates. It also asserted that the current moment is “uniquely suited to Vice President Harris and a broad coalition already in motion”. But not everyone agrees it’s Harris’s time to shine. Numerous Democratic candidates have publicly stated that they don’t want Harris’s toxic brand anywhere near their elections. El-Sayed, meanwhile, seems to have decided that an alliance with Harris is mutually beneficial. It gives the progressive candidate an inroad into the establishment and might help him win more support with Black voters. Harris, who alienated many progressives and Arab Americans by her stance on Gaza, clearly thinks that associating with El-Sayed might improve her reputation among that cohort of voters. El-Sayed has said he opposes military aid to Israel and termed the situation in Gaza a genocide – as have numerous human rights groups and genocide experts. El-Sayed isn’t the only progressive that Harris appears to be trying to build bridges with. Last year, Harris offered only the most lukewarm of endorsements for Zohran Mamdani, stating: “He’s the Democratic nominee, and he should be supported.” Now that it’s clear that Mamdani embodies the political zeitgeist, she’s a lot more keen to be besties. In early July, Axios reported that Harris called up the New York mayor a couple of days after three leftwing candidates he’d endorsed won their primaries over establishment-backed candidates. In fact, Harris has been working the phones pretty hard. The same Axios piece noted that she’d reached out to a number of pro-Palestinian activists and Arab American leaders including James Zogby, founder and president of the Arab American Institute. He told Slate this week that the two had had a “long talk”, which he felt good about. In 2024, the Democrats took progressives for granted. They assumed that young progressives would show up to vote blue no matter who, even when the party treated them with disdain. Instead many of these voters stayed home. The Democrats are still loath to admit that Gaza was a factor in their defeat: a 2024 autopsy report released by the Democratic National Committee did not mention the issue once. However, it looks like Harris is waking up to the realization that her almost unconditional support for Israel hurt her in the previous election and is something she will have to rectify if she wants to run again. Particularly since polls show a record 60% of US adults now have an unfavourable view of Israel and the vast majority of Democrats support an arms embargo. Is all this too little too late for the former nominee’s brand? I don’t know. But it’s certainly too late for the tens of thousands of Palestinians the Biden-Harris administration were complicit in killing. The murder of nine women causes a reckoning in South Africa The bodies of nine women have been found across the Ekurhuleni district, east of Johannesburg, over the past two months. Some were naked or partially clothed. The apparent murders, which may be connected, have reignited protests about the country’s femicide rate, which is five times higher than the global average. Hundreds of demonstrators marched through Cape Town on Thursday, demanding an end to gender-based violence. Afghan cyclist who disguised herself as a man to train wins Asian Games silver Fariba Hashimi was attacked with stones and had to train while disguised as a man when she first started cycling. Now based in Italy, Hashimi won an Asian Games silver medal on Tuesday and hopes to compete in the 2028 Los Angeles games. A Republican senator has warned that furries are infiltrating the aviation community “It’s terrifying when you think about this,” the senator Tommy Tuberville said this week. “When you walk onto a commercial flight, it’s possible that the pilot flying your plane could have a deranged fetish of dressing up like an animal.” Tuberville seems to be referencing an incident in April when pilots were heard making “meow” sounds over an air traffic control frequency at Ronald Reagan Washington national airport. Is it possible they were maybe just mucking around? Or have the friendly really skies been taken over by a dastardly coalition of furries? Masked lesbian infighting went ultra-viral this week I wrote about the Last Ditch drama here. The dangers of AI are already here “The future is already here – it’s just unevenly distributed,” the science fiction writer William Gibson once said. And that is very true of AI. “We don’t have to wait to see how AI will bring about unprecedented death and destruction, because we’ve already witnessed its unleashing,” Granate Kim and Mohamed Hussein write in the Guardian. Six-year-old Chinese girl ‘sets new women’s Rubik’s Cube world record’ Lian Yunzhi is reportedly “the first female speedcuber to average under 4.5 seconds”. A day in the life of a pregnant woman in Gaza Sitting in her tent, warding off rats, Alaa watches videos of her three children, killed in an Israeli airstrike, on her cracked smartphone. She gave birth to a new baby boy, Waseem, shortly after the Guardian published this piece. Ed Sheeran’s shows at Gillette Stadium canceled due to nor’easter A hilarious development in the Ed “I’m not complicit in genocide” Sheeran tour story. Even the weather is sick of hearing him whine. Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

webTitle: ‘The weaker he gets, the more dangerous he gets’: Trump lashes out as his power wanes

fields.headline: ‘The weaker he gets, the more dangerous he gets’: Trump lashes out as his power wanes
fields.trailText: Trump tries to dominate at the UN as his approval ratings plummet and even some Republicans distance themselves from him
fields.bodyText: Donald Trump stood before the United Nations on Tuesday and threatened to “annihilate” Iran. Yet even as the most powerful man on the planet flexed his military muscles, he was powerless to keep the gravitational pull of domestic politics at bay. Heading into the UN building in New York, the US president was questioned by Kaitlan Collins, an anchor at CNN, which he had banned from the White House before a judge ruled against him. “I’m surprised that CNN is here covering me,” the 80-year-old snapped. “You should not be here covering me.” The lashing-out was a reminder that even Trump, who has expanded executive power and dominated the national consciousness, finds some things beyond his control. Indeed, 20 months into his second term, there is a widening gap between the president’s self-perceived invincibility and the reality of his waning influence. Federal courts are reining him in. Congressional Republicans are straying from the script. Poll numbers are tumbling to historic depths, driven by persistent inflation, rising fuel costs and an increasingly unpopular war in Iran. For the first time since his improbable political resurrection, Trump’s aura of authority is fading. Rick Wilson, a longtime Republican strategist, prophesied: “This is the beginning of the end. This is the decline. As powerful and transgressive as he’s been, the country does not have a positive outlook right now. In fact, the negativity and pessimism among voters has reached a point that is unparalleled since Jimmy Carter.” Trump’s self-belief never wavers. He faced four criminal cases and two assassination attempts before winning the 2024 election. He has lived by a mantra of “it will all work out well in the end” while his supporters wear hats that state: “Trump was right about everything.” Yet he has had a rough month. The Federal Reserve defied him on interest rates. The supreme court blocked his administration’s attempt to impose new restrictions on mail-in ballots for November’s midterm elections. One judge prevented him adding his name to the Kennedy Center, prompting him to threaten the national arts complex with demolition; another judge blocked his ban on three news outlets from the White House grounds, ordering the administration to “immediately return, reinstate and restore” their access. Now even Trump’s dependable power base, the Republican party, is showing cracks amid fears that he will cost them seats in November. In Florida, his home state, gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds quietly scrubbed most Trump references from his campaign website, while the congresswoman María Elvira Salazar ran campaign advertisements openly declaring that federal immigration enforcement had gone “too far” and asserting that Latino voters “feel betrayed”. Wilson, a co-founder of the Lincoln Project, an anti-Trump group, sees a herd mentality among congressional Republicans and compares the current mood to a wildlife documentary. “It needs a David Attenborough voiceover,” he said. “It’s like the gazelles wandering the savannah. They’re sniffing the wind now and they smell something in the wind. They know it’s a predator but they don’t know what to do about it yet. What they haven’t realised is that the predator has been among them all along. The risk factor that they face now is Trump.” For nearly a decade, elected Republicans maintained a posture of submission, fearful of drawing a primary challenger or a scathing post on Truth Social. But with the elections looming and control of Congress hanging in the balance, self-preservation is rapidly overriding loyalty to the president. Wilson said: “Now it’s reached the point where the magic doesn’t work any more. There’s no political upside from a president who is at 29% approval rating in some polls, has presided over a disastrous war, and has ended up raising energy prices and food prices – all the things that they can’t spin away. “The voters now have very much put that together. They associate the war with Trump. They associate the gas prices with Trump. They associate the grocery prices with Trump.” This creates a vicious circle, Wilson argues. “The more he becomes a liability, the more he acts out. The more he demands loyalty from people and doesn’t get it, the more he demands loyalty from people and doesn’t get it. Everything was handed to him for a decade by that party and, now that they’re paying the price, they’ve decided this has got a little too hairy.” Faced with shrinking authority and a hostile economic landscape, Trump has reverted to his trusted playbook: manufacturing spectacle, picking cultural fights and raging against the press. His recent decision to ban the news outlets CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House campus following critical coverage was viewed by critics not as a display of strength, but a symptom of deep frustration. The administration rejects such charges and insists that the president’s agenda is succeeding. Davis Ingle, a White House spokesperson, said in an email: “President Trump is the unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party, and he is committed to maintaining Republican majorities in Congress. “The president signed the largest working-class tax cuts in history, lowered the cost of prescription drugs, sealed the border, drove violent crime to the lowest level in nearly a century, unleashed an energy revolution, added more than a million private-sector jobs, and sent Americans’ 401(k)s climbing to record highs,” he added. “The choice has never been more clear: doubling down on President Trump’s winning, commonsense agenda or the Democrats’ extreme liberal policies and obstruction.” But the trend lines are only set to worsen for Trump. If Democrats gain control of the House of Representatives, they plan to launch investigations into how he has allegedly abused his office to enrich his family, grant favours to supporters, hollow out the federal government and carry out expensive construction projects. The attention economy, meanwhile, will inexorably shift to the 2028 presidential race and the question of succession. Bill Galston, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution thinktank in Washington, said the inevitable shift of focus toward potential candidates – such as the vice-president, JD Vance, or the secretary of state, Marco Rubio – will be cause for friction. “Nothing will drive him crazier than the shift of the spotlight away from him,” said Galston, a former domestic policy adviser to Bill Clinton. “The prospect of passing the torch, giving up the spotlight, is intensely painful for him. It’s his oxygen. Will he be able to breathe, spiritually and emotionally speaking, without it?” Trump is not the first president to run into trouble after winning re-election. From Richard Nixon’s Watergate downfall to Clinton’s impeachment and George W Bush’s quagmire in Iraq, second terms have historically served as the graveyard of presidential ambition. Allan Lichtman, author of a new book, Great American Presidents: The Twelve Who Transformed the Nation, calls it “the second term curse”. He noted: “Second terms have been remarkably difficult for presidents.” Lichtman, a history professor at American University in Washington, believes that Trump is driven by two things: money and glory. “He cannot stand not being the centre of attention and that’s dangerous,” he said. “I don’t care much about his verbal lashing-out; I don’t think that helps him at all. But who knows what crazy things he might do to reassert attention on him? And that’s frightening. “Never underestimate the power of the president. Just because Republicans are criticising him, his poll numbers are low, prospects for Republicans look dim, doesn’t mean he doesn’t have enormous power – and he is certainly quite willing to use that power unconstrained. He doesn’t care about the courts and doesn’t care about the Congress.” From this perspective, Trump’s last refuge will be the unchecked use of executive authority, a politicised justice department and a sweeping pardon power. With nothing to lose in his final two years, he could go out all guns blazing. Charlie Sykes, a conservative author and broadcaster, said: “Donald Trump fears irrelevance more than anything and he’ll rage against it as long as he can. The notion that he will go quietly would be incredibly naive. “We’re headed for a collision between a lame duck who has no respect for the constitutional norms and an opposition that may have some power to hold him accountable. The paradox is the weaker he gets, the more dangerous he gets.”

webTitle: US supreme court rejects Republican-drawn midterm map in Missouri for third time – as it happened

fields.headline: US supreme court rejects Republican-drawn midterm map in Missouri for third time – as it happened
fields.trailText: Long-running fight over Trump-backed maps takes another turn as absentee voting is already under way in Missouri. This blog is now closed.
fields.bodyText: This concludes our live coverage of the second Trump administration for today. Here are the latest developments: The White House has blocked CNN from traveling aboard Air Force One on Saturday, impeding its TV press pool duties in the latest escalation of the administration’s battle with the news media. The primary White House television pool today resumed filming administration events after a court ruling temporarily overturned a Trump administration ban on CNN. More here. Donald Trump is canceling nearly $1bn in spending approved by Congress, the White House announced, using a rare and contested power to axe funding for immigrant services and diversity-focused initiatives. More here. Dale Caldwell, the lieutenant governor of New Jersey, resigned from his position, after the release of a report accusing him of sexually harassing a female staffer, among other ethics violations. Thomas Calcagni, a lawyer for Caldwell, said in a statement they would “continue to forcefully challenge the report”. More here. The supreme court turned away an attempt to use a new Missouri congressional map backed by Donald Trump, putting an end to a long-running legal dispute as absentee voting is under way in the midterm elections. More here. The White House defended its decision to use taxpayer funds to buy airtime on Fox News for a White House-produced, pro-Trump ad that some Democrats said could be illegal government propaganda aimed at influencing voters in the upcoming midterm elections. More here. Donald Trump went on a social media posting spree on Friday night, posting 18 self-promotional videos and images on his Truth Social account in less than 30 minutes. Among the images was a meme apparently intended to show him as a resolute leader, standing at attention and saluting during a US military flyover in Maryland on Wednesday as he greeted China’s president, Xi Jinping. That edited image contrasted sharply with a news photograph taken during the flyover, which showed that, in reality, Trump had actually visibly winced as the a B-1 bomber passed low overhead. US senators have introduced legislation aimed at cutting down warrantless or specious ICE arrests, and curbing the agency’s ability to indefinitely detain immigrants who do not pose any danger to their communities. The new legislation, shared exclusively with the Guardian, would require immigration officers to obtain an administrative warrant from a supervisor outlining a probable cause for detaining someone. Such a warrant must also be presented to each person who is detained, the bill says, alongside notice of when the detainee must appear in immigration court. The bill would require a bond hearing within 24 hours of any warrantless arrests, and custody review of every noncitizen in immigration detention every 60 days by an immigration judge or US district judge – ideally ensuring that detainees are not held in ICE custody indefinitely without clear cause. Read the full story here: A White House note confirmed earlier reports that CNN will not be flying on Air Force One on Saturday, despite being scheduled to serve as the pool reporter covering the president for major television networks. According to CNN, the network had been penciled in to fly aboard the president’s plane on his trip to Tennessee for a college football game as part of the White House TV press pool. The White House note does not list an outlet replacing CNN. Donald Trump is canceling nearly $1b in spending approved by Congress, with most of the cuts focused on health and human services programs that serve refugees and unaccompanied minors accused of being in the country illegally, per the AP. The White House is using a rare and contested power to axe the funding. The Office of Management and Budget described the funding cut as focused on “the most harmful government spending.” Republican senator Susan Collins, chair of the Senate appropriations committee, said in a statement that the action came “without warning or consultation.” “Any effort to rescind appropriated funds without congressional approval is a clear violation of the law,” Collins wrote in a post on social media. “I will work with my colleagues to address these illegal actions.” The White House blocked CNN from traveling with President Donald Trump on Air Force One for a Saturday trip to Knoxville, Tennessee, the Washington Post reports. The report comes after CNN, MS NOW and Politico were banned from White House grounds last week. A federal judge temporarily restored access early Thursday, but journalists for CNN and MS Now were denied access to the White House state dinner in honor of Xi Jinping later that day. US television networks resumed coverage of President Donald Trump’s White House events on Friday. Following the supreme court’s decision to turn away an attempt to use a new Missouri congressional map backed by Donald Trump, challengers of the map said “the courts have now made clear that voters — not politicians — decide who represents them.” “This case should never have reached the Supreme Court three times, but we’re glad that the final outcome of these cases is Missourians having the opportunity to vote under a lawful map this fall,” said Mark Gaber, senior director of redistricting at Campaign Legal Center. “The people of Missouri have the right to go to the polls and reject the State’s attempt to gerrymander their congressional districts, and the Supreme Court has now confirmed, for the third time in as many weeks, that the State’s unlawful districts cannot be used this November,” said Ming Cheung, senior staff attorney with the ACLU’s Voting Rights Project. “Voting has already begun, and all efforts to cause confusion and chaos must cease. This saga began in 2025 when politicians tried to rig the map and take away representation from Kansas City residents, but the courts have now made clear that voters — not politicians — decide who represents them.” Campaign Legal Center, the ACLU of Missouri and ACLU Voting Rights Project filed amicus briefs at the Missouri Supreme Court. Here’s more on the supreme court’s decision: The White House on Friday defended its decision to use taxpayer funds to buy airtime on Fox News for a White House-produced, pro-Trump ad that some Democrats said could be illegal government propaganda aimed at influencing voters in the upcoming midterm elections. In a lengthy statement sent to news outlets, the White House press office insisted that versions of the ad, which feature audio of Trump urging voters to help him “defeat communism” and a whirlwind video review of his second term, were simply routine “public service announcements” like those produced by previous administrations. However, while the Trump administration ad features the president in almost every frame, and includes words of praise for him offered by a prominent supporter during the 2024 campaign, none of the advertising from three prior administrations the White House called similar featured any partisan messaging or showed images of Trump’s predecessors. By contrast, the 30-second version of the pro-Trump ad broadcast on Fox News this week uses audio of Trump telling supporters in Las Vegas last month: “Together we will defeat communism, socialism and Marxism in America,” and a rapid-fire montage of images of Trump beneath the onscreen text: “America will never be a communist country,” as a chorus sings the words “love me”, taken from a song of that name by JMSN. In the original speech, Trump explicitly identified the enemy as “Dumocrat communists in Congress”. The last 10 seconds of the ad include text at the bottom the screen saying: “Paid for by the US government.” The ad aired on Fox News this week as Trump hosted the leader of the world’s largest communist nation, China, for a lavish state visit. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) wrongly identified 185 people on Nevada’s voter rolls as non-citizens, state officials said this week, escalating concerns over the shoddy methodology the government is using to raise fear about non-citizen voting ahead of the midterm elections. In July, Donald Trump gave a speech saying DHS had found a combined 278,000 non-citizens on the rolls in Nevada, California, Pennsylvania and New Jersey. Follow-up letters to each of those states weakened the claim, saying there only could be as many as 278,000 non-citizens on the rolls, including up to 15,903 in Nevada. In August, DHS officials told staffers in the Nevada secretary of state’s office that they had reviewed the numbers and confirmed only 185 were non-citizens. DHS officials said they still needed to review more than 14,000 records. But on Wednesday, Nevada election officials said they had reviewed the 185 records DHS sent them and confirmed they were US citizens. “As for the 185 individuals, our records indicate that they were citizens. You have provided nothing of substance to suggest otherwise,” Greg Ott, a deputy attorney general, wrote to DHS this week in an email obtained by the Guardian through a public records request. The message was first reported by the New York Times and Nevada Independent. In a statement from the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, chair Suzan DelBene said the supreme court’s decision to lift restrictions on a federal voter database before November’s elections is “a lever for Republicans to pull to misinform and scare away legal voters.” “Republicans are running scared,” said DelBene. “They know they’ve lost the American people, and are resorting to doing everything they can to stop US citizens from casting ballots.” “At a minimum, today’s ruling is a lever for Republicans to pull to misinform and scare away legal voters from exercising their constitutional right,” DelBene added. “At its worst, it may inspire sinister Republican officials to try and illegally purge swaths of American citizens off the voter rolls weeks before the election. It won’t work, and the American people won’t stand for it.” My colleague George Chidi reported on the supreme court’s decision: The Supreme Court has blocked Missouri for a third time from using a Republican-drawn congressional map in the November midterm elections, per the AP. The justices granted a request by the map’s opponents to suspend lower court decisions that had required the reconfigured US House of ⁠Representatives district boundaries to be used in the 3 November midterm elections. The back-and-forth is occurring as absentee voting is already underway in Missouri. President Donald Trump is reportedly visiting Alabama for a political rally next week, Politico reports. It’s a questionable move given the high stakes of this year’s midterm elections. With polls showing Democratic candidates holding a lead, rallying in a reliably red state like Alabama is a curious move. Two people who spoke with Politico, which reported the news on Thursday, said the event is scheduled for 2 October in Mobile, Alabama, but the plans have not yet been finalized and are subject to change. In a letter to Donald Trump, a group of more than a dozen senators on both sides of the aisle questioned Russian President Vladimir Putin’s invitation to the December G20 summit scheduled in Miami, expressing “serious concern” as the Russia-Ukraine war continues. Senators including Mitch McConnell, John Cornyn, Sheldon Whitehouse, Roger Wicker, among others, signed the letter. “We write to express our serious concern regarding reports that Russian President Vladimir Putin has been invited to attend the Group of Twenty (G20) Leaders’ Summit on December 14 and 15 in Miami, Florida,” reads the letter. “President Putin bears sole responsibility for launching Russia’s full-scale war of aggression against Ukraine,” the letter continues. “Allowing him to participate in a G20 Summit in the United States raises serious concerns about legitimizing and normalizing a government that continues to attack Ukrainian civilian targets every day.” The invitation was announced by Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, during a press conference in New York on Wednesday. Moments after Dale Caldwell resigned from his position as lieutenant governor of New Jersey, his lawyer Thomas Calcagni said in a statement that they would “continue to forcefully challenge the report” that accuses Caldwell of sexually harassing a staffer and violating state ethics rules. Dr. Caldwell’s resignation, submitted to put an end to the targeted campaign to discredit his character, does not in any way diminish our outrage concerning the investigative process and its specious findings,” Calcagni said. “Counsel is fully exploring all legal remedies to ensure a true, balanced, and unbiased record.” My colleague Ariana Baio is reporting the latest details on Caldwell’s resignation: If the Beijing meeting between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in May was the “stalemate summit”, the second round of talks between the presidents of the US and China this week seemed to give up entirely on the idea of breakthroughs. Instead, it was described as a celebration of “diplotainment” rather than diplomacy, where pomp prevailed over progress and where one of the main outcomes was the news that two giant pandas would soon be sent from China to Atlanta zoo. Trump rolled out the red carpet for Xi’s arrival on Wednesday and broke with decades of precedent to meet the Chinese leader at Joint Base Andrews. Thus began a three-day state visit that involved a tour of Trump’s new helipad and the Marine One helicopter, and a 90-minute meeting that Trump described as “great” and that revealed, according to Trump, that Xi “has great interest in granite”. “The biggest takeaway is that Trump has been displaying an extraordinary degree of deference to Xi Jinping,” said Julian Gewirtz, who served as a senior China official in the Biden administration. But what of actual substance? Expectations going into the summit were low. But the outcomes somehow still fell short. One of the biggest issues in the US-China relationship is trade. Last year, as Trump unveiled successive rounds of tariffs on Chinese goods, the White House accused China of unfair practices that it said contributed to the loss of 3.7m US jobs and inflated the trade deficit. The tariffs were supposed to suppress the volume of Chinese imports to the US and put pressure on China. To some degree, they worked. The US trade deficit with China in 2025 fell to $200bn, down from nearly $300bn in 2024. But experts have noted that some of this shortfall is made up for by Chinese goods being shipped to the US via third countries, a trend underlined by the fact that China’s trade surplus surpassed a record $1tn last year. With the US and China accounting for 43% of global GDP, their trade war has far-reaching implications for the world economy. So it was a relief not just to Beijing and to US consumers when the two countries agreed a temporary truce in Busan last year. That truce is due to expire in November. China, where the economy is heavily reliant on exports, was reported to be pushing for the truce to be extended until the end of Trump’s term, in January 2029. On Thursday, it was revealed that Xi’s first state visit to the US in more than a decade had resulted in a mere two-month extension. That reflects “the lack of preparation for this summit beyond the pomp and circumstance”, said Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at the Asia Society. William Yang, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group, said: “This summit largely achieved symbolism and ritualism over substance. That is very clear.” The short extension “reflects the level of fundamental differences that still exist between the two countries over a variety of issues”. China’s most powerful response to Trump’s tariffs was the decision to block the export of rare earths, critical minerals vital to US manufacturing and military supply chains. That seemed to skewer Trump’s leverage over China. Gewirtz said: “Beijing’s retaliation … seems to have had a profound effect on [Trump] and his administration’s willingness to take risks vis-a-vis China.” Apart from the trade war agreement, the summit failed to achieve any meaningful progress on thorny issues in the US-China relationship such as artificial intelligence, Taiwan, the wars in Iran and Ukraine, and human rights. On Taiwan, which Beijing considers to be the most important issue in the relationship, Xi put pressure on Trump to weaken the US’s support for the self-governing island that China claims as its own. According to the Chinese readout of the Xi-Trump meeting, Xi told Trump he hoped “the US side will adhere to the correct position of opposing Taiwan independence”. For the US to state that it “opposes” Taiwanese independence would be a rhetorical shift from the current position of “does not support” such a claim, and would be a move welcomed by Beijing. Trump has not yet commented on whether he agreed to such a statement. But it does seem he is no closer to approving a $14bn arms sale package for Taiwan, a sale that Beijing would like to see disappear completely. On Thursday, US Senate Democrats lambasted Trump for opting for “pageantry over purpose” and for failing to deliver agreements on “the economic and security issues that will shape America’s future”. Trump ignored recent warnings about the dangers posed by AI, writing on social media on Thursday: “I want to leave it exactly where it is,” adding: “That is China’s position also.” For China, the lack of big news from the visit is a win in itself. “The summit went excellently from the Chinese perspective,” Thomas said. Xi “got a huge amount of respect from the American president, the full state visit treatment [and] really great images beaming back to China of the Chinese and the American presidents interacting as peers on the global stage, without having to make any meaningful concessions or compromises.” New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill announced this afternoon that Dale Caldwell, her lieutenant governor, had resigned in light of an ethics probe that concluded he had sexually harassed a staffer and violated ethics rules. Caldwell, a pastor and former university president with a long career in education, was found to have broken the rules of his office when he lobbied for a promotion for a government employee who he was in a romantic relationship with, and brought guests to ticketed events without paying, according to the report commissioned by Sherrill’s office . He also allegedly made romantic advances on the friend of a young female staffer in that staffer’s presence, and, when declined, told the staffer: “you young women are looking for young sperm.” The findings of that report prompted Sherrill, a Democrat, to request Caldwell’s resignation on Thursday when she publicized the report’s findings. In an interview with The New York Times before Sherrill’s press conference, Caldwell insisted he was not resigning because of the report, whose contents he disputed. “It’s false,” Caldwell said of the report to the outlet. “I’m resigning because I don’t want to be a distraction to the administration.” In a post to social media shortly after Xi Jinping’s departure from the White House, Trump confirmed that he planned to meet twice more with the Chinese president this year. Trump said he first planned to meet President Xi in China during November’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, scheduled to take place in Shenzhen. They’ll meet again in December during the G20 in Miami. “The meeting was one of Friendship, Strength, and Success, for both China and the USA,” Trump said. He added: “Much has been, and will be, accomplished. I look forward to our next meeting!” The statement is a friendly coda to Xi’s first official state visit (the most formal designation such a diplomatic trip can receive) since the tail end of the Obama administration, in which Trump gave the Chinese leader an uncharacteristically warm welcome, including a red carpet greeting on the tarmac and a lavish dinner filled with dignitaries, Trump allies and business executives. The pleasantries may have papered over long-simmering tensions between the two countries, but what conclusions, if any, were reached during the pair’s White House talks remains unclear. Trump has said the two sides discussed the Iran war, as the administration seeks China’s buy-in to a plan to economically isolate the country. The emergency docket, sometimes also referred to as the “shadow docket”, is where plaintiffs can request immediate relief from the supreme court in consequential cases. Justices can quickly grant or dismiss requests without conducting the same legal review that is typically required in merit cases or providing a lengthy explanation to the public. The Trump administration has used the method to rapidly push forward the US president’s agenda. Diplomatic editor Iran’s seven-day timetable to reopen the strait of Hormuz and start talks on its nuclear programme has been pitched as a deal that could rapidly extricate Donald Trump from a political crisis but requires the US president to make difficult concessions. In the five days left before the proposed reopening of the strait, which is expected to relieve pressure on global energy markets, Trump would need to lift Iranian asset freezes, permit Iran to export its oil and, probably most difficult of all, order Benjamin Netanyahu to end Israel’s attacks on Hezbollah in Lebanon, thus achieving the “ceasefire on all fronts”. Iranian diplomats in New York said they thought a three-hour meeting earlier this week with the US envoy Steve Witkoff in which they laid out the seven-day plan was productive, but were doubtful the US would deliver. Iran nevertheless feels it has done the diplomatic spadework, taking the proposal to China for endorsement and ensuring that Oman, located on the south side of the strait, was also on board. The foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, explained that the idea was to take the elements of the Iran-US memorandum of understanding that Trump signed in June and repackage and accelerate the process since, as they understood it, Trump had come to hate the MoU. “The conditions we have asked the US to meet is nothing new, nothing more than what was already in the Islamabad agreement, which was signed by the US president,” Araghchi said. But what is new is the speed. In the first four to five days under this timetable, the US would have to lift the naval blockade on Iran’s oil ports, restore the waiver that lifted sanctions on Iran’s oil exports, end the war on all fronts and permit the release of some of Iran’s frozen assets. On the sixth day, the strait of Hormuz would be reopened by Iran, with ships using a new route designated by Oman and Iran. And on the next day, negotiations would start on the future of Iran’s civil nuclear programme, including a protocol to allow UN nuclear inspectors back in to look at Iran’s damaged sites and the stockpile of highly enriched uranium. This accelerates the point at which nuclear talks would begin, from 60 days in the June agreement to seven. It is a difficult deal for Trump to swallow since the strait would reopen largely on Iran’s terms, with the new route predominantly going through Iranian waters. Saudi Arabia is also concerned that the route deal is bilateral between Iran and Oman, and not with the Gulf states as joint signatories. Trump says he has a choice to make between the annihilation of Iran and engagement – an engagement that, he says with typical hyperbole, could make Iran one of the great countries of the world. In reality, the judgment he has to make is more prosaic. Is he prepared to go back to war with Iran after the midterms and, if not, does he believe the US can squeeze the Iranian economy so hard that the leadership will succumb. Sooknanan had blocked the use of the tool, saying it violated Americans’ privacy rights and could result in voters being wrongly removed from the rolls. A federal appeals court let her order stand.
